title: Mellophone, giving up banjo, and the crowds at Bond Hill House
summary: He puts the banjo aside for trumpet and mellophone, and describes dancing crowds, the house becoming Lorman's Gardens, and the band's make-up.

story.theme_name: Banjo, guitar and the rhythm section: instruments and players
story.community_name: Fiddlers and reading violinists of New Orleans

blocks.x: Did you play--- well, you did play the hot stuff---
Yes, but you see, very few people
were playing the mellophone at that time. There was a guy named Dudley Fessdick, who was around in those days and he was playing-- he was playing the mellophone and---
You were all through with the banjo by this time--- weren't you?
Well, I was just putting it aside.
Yeah because when I heard a guy like Carl Clauve - unbelievable banjo - he could play melody and harmony and lead - it sounded like a piano. So, I then concentrated on the trumpet and the mellophone.
The kind of music you played then was you were playing for dancing. That was---

Oh - well, that was the big thing in those days. They danced to jazz music in those days. And, it was nothing to see five hundred couples out on that floor in that Bond Hill House. And, it was an old wooden building with an outdoor shell and what is amazing when I think back, we did so much business that summer for that place that they torn the building down and built a great big brick one on the money they made with our band that summer. And, it became then - it became "Lorman's Gardens".
They changed the name from Bond Hill House to Lorman's Gardens and we played in there. And, oh, it was very elegant there.
You had what about - a ten - twelve
piece band - was that what it was?
I think it was ten pieces---
Yeah and Art Hicks played the violin.

I think with Art it was eleven. You know, he was a leader. We had three saxophones and three brass and four rhythm. And, the leader played the violin. Well, it was that summer that Carl introduced me to Bix---
